kc_context.canonical_name: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets
kc_context.definition_or_summary:
When two classification models are evaluated on two independent test sets, their observed error rates can be compared to determine whether the difference in performance is statistically significant.

If model M1 has error rate e1 on a test set of size n1 and model M2 has error rate e2 on an independent test set of size n2, the observed difference is

d = e1 - e2.

For sufficiently large test sets, the error rates can be approximated by normal distributions, and the variance of the difference can be estimated as

σd² ≈ e1(1 - e1)/n1 + e2(1 - e2)/n2.

A confidence interval for the true difference in error rates can then be used to judge statistical significance. If the confidence interval includes 0, the observed difference is not statistically significant at that confidence level.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with specific statistical tests like McNemar or Friedman tests which may be used for the actual comparison of performance metrics.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Accuracy is a traditional measure of classification performance that represents the fraction of instances whose class labels are predicted correctly.

For an entire classifier:

Accuracy = number of correct predictions / total number of predictions.

In the specific context of a classification rule, rule accuracy, also called the confidence factor, is the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels equal the rule's target class.

Accuracy can be misleading when the test data has class imbalance because a classifier can achieve high accuracy by predicting the majority class while performing poorly on the minority class.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Precision and Recall, which are often used as alternatives when accuracy is misleading due to skew.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Test sample size determines how precisely a classifier's performance can be estimated from a test set.

A larger test sample reduces the standard error and therefore produces a narrower confidence interval around the measured accuracy. This means that the accuracy estimate is more precise and less affected by sampling variation.

A larger test sample does not automatically make the classifier more accurate or better. It mainly gives greater confidence in the estimate of its performance. Test sample size can also affect statistical significance when comparing classifiers, because with sufficiently large samples even relatively small performance differences may become statistically significant.

The Laplace estimator is a method for estimating categorical conditional probabilities that prevents unseen attribute-class combinations from receiving probability zero.

Formula:
P(X_i = c | y) = (n_c + 1) / (n + v)

where:
n_c = number of training instances in class y with X_i = c
n = total number of training instances belonging to class y
v = number of possible values of attribute X_i

Its purpose is to avoid the zero-frequency problem, where one zero conditional probability can make the entire class-conditional product zero.

Training error may underestimate generalization error, especially for complex models that overfit the training data. A separate validation set can therefore be used to estimate generalization performance during model selection or pruning.

Decision-tree pruning methods attempt to improve generalization by controlling model complexity. Different methods estimate or control generalization error differently. For example, reduced-error pruning evaluates performance on a validation set, whereas pessimistic error estimation combines training error with a penalty for tree complexity. Other pruning approaches include cost-complexity pruning.

For reduced-error pruning, the true class labels in the validation set provide the ground truth against which the tree's predictions are compared, rather than the training leaf counts or the predictions themselves.

kc_context.definition_or_summary: The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is an oversampling approach used to address class imbalance by generating synthetic positive instances rather than simply duplicating existing ones. kc_context.definition_or_summary:
K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that divides a data set into a user-specified number K of clusters, with each cluster represented by a centroid.

The basic algorithm is:

1. Choose K initial centroids.
2. Assign each data point to its closest centroid.
3. Recompute the centroid of each cluster from the points assigned to it.
4. Repeat the assignment and centroid-update steps until no points change clusters, or equivalently, until the centroids no longer change.

For standard Euclidean K-Means, the centroid of a cluster is the mean of its points, and the objective is to minimize the total sum of squared errors (SSE), which measures the squared distances of points from their assigned centroids.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Centroid initialization sensitivity refers to the dependence of the final K-Means clustering on the initial positions chosen for the centroids.

Because K-Means converges only to a local minimum of its objective function, different initial centroid choices can lead to different cluster assignments and different total SSE values. Some starting configurations may lead to a good or globally optimal clustering, while others may lead to a suboptimal local minimum.

A common way to reduce this problem is to run K-Means several times with different initial centroids and select the clustering with the lowest SSE. Other initialization methods can also be used to obtain better starting centroids.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
The SSE optimization criterion is the objective used by standard Euclidean K-Means to evaluate and improve a clustering. It measures the total squared distance between every data point and the centroid of the cluster to which that point is assigned.

SSE = sum over all clusters of the squared distances between each point and its cluster centroid.

K-Means tries to minimize this total SSE. Assigning each point to its nearest centroid reduces SSE for the current centroids, and recomputing each centroid as the mean of its assigned points further minimizes SSE for the current cluster assignments.

For a fixed value of K, a smaller SSE indicates a better clustering according to the K-Means objective.

kc_context.canonical_name: Comparing Two Models on Independent Test Sets
kc_context.definition_or_summary:
When two classification models are evaluated on two independent test sets, their observed error rates can be compared to determine whether the difference in performance is statistically significant.

If model M1 has error rate e1 on a test set of size n1 and model M2 has error rate e2 on an independent test set of size n2, the observed difference is

d = e1 - e2.

For sufficiently large test sets, the error rates can be approximated by normal distributions, and the variance of the difference can be estimated as

σd² ≈ e1(1 - e1)/n1 + e2(1 - e2)/n2.

A confidence interval for the true difference in error rates can then be used to judge statistical significance. If the confidence interval includes 0, the observed difference is not statistically significant at that confidence level.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with specific statistical tests like McNemar or Friedman tests which may be used for the actual comparison of performance metrics.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
When evaluating a classifier, different evaluation measures capture different aspects of performance. Measures such as precision and FPR primarily capture the effect of false positives, while recall and TPR primarily capture the effect of false negatives. Optimizing only one type of measure may therefore result in a classifier with low false negatives but high false positives, or vice versa. Measures such as the F1-measure can be used when both types of misclassification need to be taken into account.

When selecting an optimal classification-score threshold on a validation set, the choice also depends on whether the evaluation measure is sensitive to class skew. For skew-sensitive measures such as precision or F1, the skew of the validation set should be similar to the expected skew of the test set. Alternatively, an estimate of the test-set skew can be combined with the TPR and TNR obtained on the validation set to estimate the test-set confusion matrix and the corresponding evaluation measure, which can then be used for threshold selection.

Understanding these mechanisms is critical as the assumptions made about missingness and the patterns of missing values determine which treatment methods can be correctly applied.

A one-sided test considers extreme values of the test statistic in only one direction.

A right-tailed test treats unusually large values as evidence against the null hypothesis, while a left-tailed test treats unusually small values as evidence against the null hypothesis. The p-value is therefore calculated from the corresponding single tail of the null distribution.

A two-sided test considers extreme values in both directions. Its p-value includes probabilities from both tails of the null distribution.

For example, when α = 0.05, a symmetric two-sided test has 0.025 in each tail, while a one-sided test has the full 0.05 in one tail.

The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed test statistic or something more extreme.

The significance level, α, is a predefined threshold used to decide whether a p-value is statistically significant. For a single test, the null hypothesis is rejected when the p-value is below α.

In the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for multiple hypothesis testing, the m p-values are first ordered from smallest to largest:

p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pm.

A different threshold is assigned to each ordered p-value:

αi = iα / m.

Thus, the threshold for the smallest p-value is α/m, the same as the Bonferroni threshold, while the threshold for the largest p-value is α.

The procedure finds the largest index k for which

pk ≤ kα/m,

and declares the first k ordered p-values significant.

In this way, BH provides a less conservative alternative to Bonferroni by controlling the False Discovery Rate while generally providing greater statistical power.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
When two classification models are evaluated on two independent test sets, their observed error rates can be compared to determine whether the difference in performance is statistically significant.

If model M1 has error rate e1 on a test set of size n1 and model M2 has error rate e2 on an independent test set of size n2, the observed difference is

d = e1 - e2.

For sufficiently large test sets, the error rates can be approximated by normal distributions, and the variance of the difference can be estimated as

σd² ≈ e1(1 - e1)/n1 + e2(1 - e2)/n2.

A confidence interval for the true difference in error rates can then be used to judge statistical significance. If the confidence interval includes 0, the observed difference is not statistically significant at that confidence level.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
The SSE optimization criterion is the objective used by standard Euclidean K-Means to evaluate and improve a clustering. It measures the total squared distance between every data point and the centroid of the cluster to which that point is assigned.

SSE = sum over all clusters of the squared distances between each point and its cluster centroid.

K-Means tries to minimize this total SSE. Assigning each point to its nearest centroid reduces SSE for the current centroids, and recomputing each centroid as the mean of its assigned points further minimizes SSE for the current cluster assignments.

For a fixed value of K, a smaller SSE indicates a better clustering according to the K-Means objective.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that divides a data set into a user-specified number K of clusters, with each cluster represented by a centroid.

The basic algorithm is:

2. Assign each data point to its closest centroid.
3. Recompute the centroid of each cluster from the points assigned to it.
4. Repeat the assignment and centroid-update steps until no points change clusters, or equivalently, until the centroids no longer change.

For standard Euclidean K-Means, the centroid of a cluster is the mean of its points, and the objective is to minimize the total sum of squared errors (SSE), which measures the squared distances of points from their assigned centroids.

K-Means tries to minimize this total SSE. Assigning each point to its nearest centroid reduces SSE for the current centroids, and recomputing each centroid as the mean of its assigned points further minimizes SSE for the current cluster assignments.

For a fixed value of K, a smaller SSE indicates a better clustering according to the K-Means objective.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Cosine similarity measures the similarity between two vectors based on the angle between them, or equivalently, how closely they point in the same direction.

It is calculated as

cos(x, y) = (x · y) / (||x|| ||y||),

where x · y is the dot product of the two vectors and ||x|| and ||y|| are their magnitudes.

A larger cosine similarity indicates greater similarity in direction. For general vectors, cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1, while for non-negative vectors such as word-count vectors it ranges from 0 to 1.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
A cluster is a group of data objects regarded as belonging together according to a particular notion of similarity, proximity, connectivity, density, or shared properties. Different clustering approaches therefore use different definitions of what constitutes a cluster.

In a graph-based definition, where nodes represent objects and links represent connections, a cluster can be defined as a connected component: a group of objects connected to one another with no connections to objects outside the group.

A specific graph-based form is a contiguity-based cluster, where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance. Consequently, each object in the cluster is closer to some other object in the same cluster than to any point in another cluster. This definition can capture irregular or intertwined clusters, but it is sensitive to noise because a small bridge of points can connect and merge two otherwise distinct clusters.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with distance-based metrics like Inter-cluster or Intra-cluster distance by focusing on connectivity rather than just distance values.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
The Rand Index is a similarity-oriented external validation measure used to compare a clustering against true class labels by examining pairs of distinct objects. It measures the proportion of object pairs for which the clustering and the class structure agree.

Specifically, f11 represents pairs that belong to the same cluster and the same class, while f00 represents pairs that belong to different clusters and different classes. The Rand Index is calculated as:

Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00).

Thus, the Rand Index gives credit both for pairs that are correctly grouped together and for pairs that are correctly separated.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
The filter-versus-wrapper trade-off in feature selection concerns how feature subsets are evaluated.

Filter methods evaluate features using criteria that are independent of the learning algorithm. They are generally faster, computationally cheaper, can handle larger data sets, and produce feature subsets that can be used with different learning algorithms.

Wrapper methods use the target learning algorithm itself to evaluate candidate feature subsets according to predictive performance. This allows them to exploit the characteristics of a particular learner and potentially obtain better feature subsets for that learner, but they require greater computational cost and can be more susceptible to overfitting.

Thus, the trade-off is mainly between the speed and generality of filters and the learner-specific predictive optimization of wrappers.

The filter approach is a feature selection method that selects features before the learning algorithm is applied.

It evaluates individual features or feature subsets using criteria that are independent of the learning algorithm, such as information, distance, dependency, consistency, or correlation measures. Features considered undesirable or redundant are filtered out, and the selected features are then supplied to the learning algorithm.

Because the selection process does not depend on a particular learning algorithm, the resulting feature subset can potentially be used with different data mining models.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
A ranker is a subcategory of filter-based feature selection that evaluates individual features using a chosen criterion, assigns each feature a score, and orders the features according to those scores.

The result is a ranked list of features rather than necessarily a final minimum feature subset. A later learning process or a user-defined threshold can then determine how many of the highest-ranked features should be retained.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Bidirectional Generation (BG) is a feature-subset generation method that performs forward and backward search concurrently.

The forward search begins with an empty selected set and adds features, while the backward search begins with the full feature set and removes features.

BG stops when one of the two search directions finds a satisfactory subset according to the specified criterion, or when the searches reach the middle of the search space.

BG combines the advantages of Sequential Forward Generation and Sequential Backward Generation and is a heuristic search method.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) and Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) which represent unidirectional search directions.

kc_context.definition_or_summary:
Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a feature-subset generation method that starts with the full set of features.

At each step, it identifies the least relevant or worst feature and removes it from the current feature set F.

The process continues until the stopping criterion is reached, such as when the removed-feature set S no longer satisfies U or when F becomes empty.

When removing the last feature causes the criterion to fail, that feature is added back so that the previous acceptable feature subset is returned.

SBG is a heuristic backward-search method because it removes features sequentially rather than evaluating every possible feature subset.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) regarding the direction of feature set modification.

kc_context.definition_or_summary: Exhaustive search is a method used to guarantee optimality by visiting all possible states. While it is the only approach that provides such a guarantee, it is possible to find an optimal subset without visiting every state by employing exact algorithms, such as branch and bound or backtracking.

sibling_contrast_notes: Contrast with Heuristic Search or Random Generation, which do not guarantee optimality.
